doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Tallmadge as mentor, layoff in 1971 and the job interviews
summary: Tallmadge's teaching and encouragement, Mancuso being let go after 1971 budget changes, and his tense faculty interview with Peter Yates and others.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: visit him all the time. I remember him telling me one time Coltrane was in town and I called him up and I says, “McCoy Tyner just took a twenty-one minute solo.” I used to time everything you know. And he goes, “I can’t do it right now, Chuck, because I’m teaching country and folk and my whole head is in country and folk.” I didn’t understand it at the time. But he did his intro courses, which were the big draws, like my jazz-rock, now American popular music is a big draw. And then he did this special course, which was, they didn’t have writing intensive, but you had to write essays and stuff. So when he was in that, you know, he stayed in that. And then when he was doing the modern jazz he’d come and see Coltrane with me and Miles and all these guys. So he was an amazing man, the fact that he would constantly call me son, and when I replaced him, I came back, because 1970 and into 1971, Rockefeller left the governorship, and all of a sudden all that money — you know we had people that went from instructor to full professor in like three years. And you got stuck with these people. It was almost too good with the money for education. That’s how strongly he believed in education. So they had to let me go in 1971 because they didn’t have the money. I was the last hired, first let go. But I kept teaching summer courses and a night course in what we now call an adjunct, while I was at Baker Hall. So when he retired I did my interviews. They didn’t want me because, as great as I did, we had Peter Yates, who wrote this book on American music, a very important book on American music, there was a lot of classical music, Peter Yates, and his wife was a world interpreter of Charles Ives. They were very important out in California. And our department hated this guy. Because he didn’t play music. He was a literature writer about music. His wife played music. He was a great writer though. He appreciated me. But they had to let me go. So now I come back from my interviews, and they’re pelting me with these questions, because they didn’t want me, most of them. They all liked me, because I didn’t spit at anybody. I wasn’t a horrible guy. But I wasn’t one of them. And Tallmadge said, “There’s no one in America can do what he’s doing right now, are you kidding? He’s way beyond all the other guys. They have bigger names. He works at this 15 hours a day.” He had to give me some time to play basketball six nights a week you know. But I really did work hard at it. And it looked good, that I was going to get the job. And Mary Fiore, who always came at me, says “Well what would you do if you had to teach theory.” She didn’t say, “What would you do, Chuck, if you had to teach theory.” She had this nasty way about her. And I says, “Well, Mary, I wouldn’t be able to do that, because I’m not trained for it. But let me say to all of you, if you had to teach Urban Blues and Rock, I can assure you, if you’re not up on what Led Zeppelin had been doing, or some of these other groups, it’s not like teaching about Mozart in the old days where you can get away with making a mistake. They will know. You will be found. And that’s dangerous. And you have to know what you’re talking about. And I can do that
